hints: Focus on drawing the dot-and-cross structure for each molecule, counting 2 electrons for every single bond and 4 for every double bond.
Start with carbon dioxide, which has two C=O double bonds, so that gives 8 bonding electrons to compare against the lone pairs on the oxygens.
Add up all the non-bonding electrons left on the outer atoms plus any on the central atom, and see which molecule gives the same total as its bonding total.
walkthrough:
**Recall what to count**

Remember, bonding electrons are the shared pairs in covalent bonds. Lone-pair electrons are the non-bonding pairs left on atoms.

Rule to use:
$$\text{bonding electrons} = 2 \times (\text{number of single bonds}) + 4 \times (\text{number of double bonds})$$

**Draw the Lewis structures**

Let's sketch each molecule quickly. $\text{BH}_3$ has 3 B-H single bonds and no lone pairs. $\text{CO}_2$ is $\text{O=C=O}$ with two double bonds. $\text{F}_2\text{O}$ is bent with two O-F single bonds. $\text{SO}_2$ is bent with two S=O bonds and one lone pair on S.

**Count bonding vs lone-pair electrons**

For $\text{CO}_2$: bonding = $2 \times 4 = 8$ electrons. Each O has 2 lone pairs, so lone-pair = $2 \times 4 = 8$ electrons. They match.

Check the others: $\text{BH}_3$ has 6 bonding and 0 lone-pair. $\text{F}_2\text{O}$ has 4 bonding and 16 lone-pair. $\text{SO}_2$ has 8 bonding and 10 lone-pair. Only one is equal.

options.A: Incorrect. BH3 has three B-H single bonds, so 6 bonding electrons, but boron has an incomplete octet and no lone pairs, so 0 lone-pair electrons. Students who forget to count zero lone pairs may guess this.
options.B: Correct. CO2 is O=C=O. Two double bonds give 8 bonding electrons. Each oxygen keeps 2 lone pairs (4 electrons each), giving 8 lone-pair electrons in total. Bonding equals lone-pair.
options.C: Incorrect. F2O has only two single bonds, so 4 bonding electrons. But oxygen has 2 lone pairs and each fluorine has 3 lone pairs, giving 4 + 12 = 16 lone-pair electrons, far more than bonding.
options.D: Incorrect. SO2 has two S=O double bonds, so 8 bonding electrons. Lone pairs are 4 on each O plus 1 lone pair on S, giving 8 + 2 = 10 lone-pair electrons. Close but not equal, a common trap if the lone pair on sulfur is missed.
